Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). Choosing between threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data has meant regulatory limits about 100× apart. The paper proposes, without implementation, formalism or experiment, that an AI system which designs further AI systems should pass on one "immutable" principle. | [LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle (2006), DOI-10.1177/1463499606061731. Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". The Y status is held only by collective acceptance, and it carries deontic powers, which are desire-independent reasons for action. Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Two revisions of the 1995 book: status indicators (after De Soto), and "free-standing Y terms" (after Barry Smith), such as corporations and money without currency. In those cases there is no X, and "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is ranked as the more general form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md)), in its parallel English printing in Papers: Revista de Sociologia 80 (2006), pp. 51–71, not in the Anthropological Theory typesetting the DOI names; worth reading as Searle's own short restatement of The Construction of Social Reality ([LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md)), and as the place where he concedes that "X counts as Y in C" is not the general form. | [LIT-489](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-489.md) | Institutions | North (1991), DOI-10.1257/jep.5.1.97. Institutions are "the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction": informal constraints (taboos, customs, codes of conduct) and formal rules (constitutions, laws, property rights). With technology they set transaction and production costs, and so the incentive structure of an economy. Tribal exchange, the Suq and the caravan trade did not evolve from within; early modern European trade did, through merchant law, bills of exchange, insurance and a state bound not to confiscate. Institutional change is path dependent because the institutional matrix has increasing returns. A narrative essay; the definition is stipulated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-392](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-392.md)); worth reading as the economist's canonical one-paragraph definition of institutions ("the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction") and as a compact statement of the transaction-cost and path-dependence programme. Unread: the argument and evidence are not known here. | Unfetched — filed 2026-10-02 from the PubMed abstract and Crossref record, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The SAGE PDF, listed as free to read, sits behind a bot challenge (HTTP 403); the PubMed record has no PMC copy; a University of North Carolina repository file returned by a search for the paper (cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/w9505f334) reset every connection, so what it holds is unknown; Semantic Scholar points only to the SAGE PDF, and CORE, OpenAlex and the Wayback Machine had no copy. It is the main harm-based rival to morality-as-cooperation, and what it argues is known here only from its abstract and from how other readings in this batch describe it. It stays Unfetched until a copy is supplied. Free copy: doi:10.1177/1088868317698288 (SAGE's PDF, listed as free to read). |
| [LIT-499](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-499.md) | Moral Foundations Theory: The Pragmatic Validity of Moral Pluralism | Graham et al. (2013), DOI-10.1016/B978-0-12-407236-7.00002-4. Moral Foundations Theory in full: a nativist, cultural-developmental, intuitionist and pluralist account with five foundations (Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity), each tied to an adaptive challenge and an existing evolutionary model. A decade of MFQ work finds liberals rely on Care and Fairness, conservatives on all five, across 12 world regions. Five criteria for "foundationhood" are proposed, and Liberty, Efficiency, Ownership and Honesty are named candidates. Harm monism (Gray) and fairness monism (Baumard) are rejected as Procrustean. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md)); worth reading as the full statement of Moral Foundations Theory and as the text to check morality-as-cooperation's comparison against. It states the theory's four claims (nativism, cultural learning, intuitionism, pluralism), reviews a decade of MFQ findings, mostly on political ideology, and offers five criteria for what counts as a foundation. By its own table the Care foundation rests on kin selection and Fairness on Trivers' reciprocal altruism, and Ownership/theft is already a named candidate, so the claim that MFT omits kin altruism, reciprocal altruism and property does not survive this text. Sanctity, the foundation morality-as-cooperation excludes, is by the same table the one with the least evidence of innate preparedness. |

Equality and Proportionality correlate weakly (mean r = .21). Purity is the foundation most related to cultural distance from the U.S. (r = .43) and to religiosity. The individualizing–binding split appears in only three of 19 national networks. | [LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md) | Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems | Ostrom (2009), Nobel lecture; AER 2010. Polycentric arrangements of many formally independent decision centres can perform better than a single hierarchy. Long-surviving common-pool resource institutions share eight design principles, among them monitoring by users or those accountable to them, graduated sanctions, local conflict resolution and nested layers. Communication and self-chosen sanctions raise cooperation in experiments. Fit to local conditions matters more than the type of regime. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-563](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-563.md)): the Nobel Prize lecture in full, from the Nobel Foundation's PDF. Worth reading as Ostrom's own summary of fifty years of work: polycentricity defined, the eight design principles of long-surviving common-pool resource institutions in their updated form, the experiments on communication and self-chosen sanctions, the field evidence on local monitoring, and the warning against single policy prescriptions. | [LIT-731](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-731.md) | Tiktok's enshittification | Doctorow (2023), Pluralistic, 21 January. Platforms die in three stages: good to users, then abusing users for business customers, then abusing both to take the value for themselves. It follows from the ease of reallocating value in a two-sided market, and lock-in, blocked interoperability and monopoly sustain it. TikTok's "heating" of chosen creators is read as stage two beginning. Remedy: end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-573](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-573.md)): in full, from the author's own blog, under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Worth reading as the essay that named enshittification and the earliest statement of it the record holds. Platforms are first good to users, then abuse users for business customers, then abuse both to claw back value; each stage is made possible by the lock-in the last one built, and blocked interoperability raises how much abuse users will bear before leaving. The remedy proposed is end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. Limits: an opinion essay argued from cases, with linked journalism and the author's own experience as evidence; its TikTok claim is a prediction. |
| [LIT-734](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-734.md) | History As Cause: Columbia and Challenger | Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003), Report Vol. I ch. 8, pp. 195–204. Foam debris and O-ring erosion followed the same trajectory: each anomaly was reinterpreted as acceptable and "in-family", and each flight without disaster justified the next. Budget and schedule pressure, a hierarchy that silenced dissent, and a dependent safety organization sustained the pattern. "History is cause": Challenger's institutional causes had not been fixed. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-578](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-578.md)): in full, from the official CAIB report as archived by the UNT Libraries CyberCemetery. Worth reading as the Board's finding that Columbia repeated Challenger's organizational cause: technical anomalies normalized one decision at a time, under budget and schedule pressure, in a hierarchy that kept dissent from rising, with a safety organization dependent on the program it oversaw. Advocates and critics of group minds share the "standard view" that ascribing attitudes tracks pre-existing causes. On McGeer's regulative view, ascription shapes its target. Ascribing knowledge to institutions, as in the collective knowledge doctrine, and issuing institutional narratives shape institutions to be more agent-like. The view stays agnostic about whether institutions really have minds. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-570.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading for a different answer to why we ascribe beliefs and knowledge to institutions: not because the ascriptions describe pre-existing states, but because, on the regulative view of folk psychology, they shape institutions to be more agent-like. Its main case is the collective knowledge doctrine in corporate criminal law, after which banks built systems to detect reporting violations. Limits: the regulative view is assumed, not argued; the causal story about banks is asserted without evidence; and the paper is agnostic about whether institutions have minds. | [LIT-743](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-743.md) | Risk management in a dynamic society: a modelling problem | Rasmussen (1997), Safety Science 27:183–213. Risk management is a control problem spanning government, regulators, companies, management, staff and work. Behaviour within a work space moves under an effort gradient and a cost gradient toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems, defences degrade unobserved under cost pressure. Accidents arise from many locally reasonable decisions. Improvement means making boundaries visible, not fighting errors. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-584.md)): the argument in full, the review of research paradigms skimmed, from the author's manuscript in DTU's repository. Worth reading for the model of drift. Under a cost gradient from management and an effort gradient from workers, activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems one actor's breach of a defence has no visible effect, so defences erode unobserved. Major accidents come from the interaction of many decision makers adapting to local pressures, not from coincident errors. Built from accident analyses; not a quantitative model. |

His advocacy of voice was "too timid": voice can be felt as a benefit, carries richer information than exit, and suits shared uncertainty; exit can be costly or uninformative. Worth reading as Hirschman's own restatement and extension of Exit, Voice, and Loyalty: voice as a recuperation mechanism that can be a benefit rather than a cost and carries richer information than exit; exit that is costly, or that signals nothing; the floor and ceiling levels of each an organization needs; and managers' interest in steering members toward the least threatening response. A retrospective on the Viable System Model. Any system able to keep its identity independently in a shared environment has five necessary and sufficient subsystems, and every viable system contains and is contained in one. The model is offered as a scientific model reached by homomorphic mapping, not an analogy. Breakdowns trace to a failing subsystem, as when Three and Five collapse without Four. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-577.md)): in full except one page, from the 1989 book reprint posted by the Cwarel Isaf Institute, which Beer co-founded. Worth reading as Beer's own retrospective on the Viable System Model. Five subsystems are claimed necessary and sufficient for any system to keep its identity independently, and the structure recurs, since every viable system contains and is contained in one. Breakdowns are diagnosed as failures of a subsystem: without System Four, Systems Three and Five collapse into each other and the system can only react. Limits: the paper declines to expound or validate the model, the copy lacks the page with the synopsis of the subsystems and its figures, and the applications are recalled, not documented. |

| [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), Science 387(6739):1153–1156, Policy Forum. Large models are best understood not as intelligent agents but as a new cultural and social technology: like writing, print and search they give access to what other people have produced, and like markets, bureaucracies and elections they make lossy, uninvertible summaries of it that can be operated on at scale. The questions that follow are the old ones about such technologies: homogenization or diversity, who gains and who loses, and which countervailing institutions emerge. Argued by historical analogy, without data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md)) from the authors' accepted version (Science galley of 25 February 2025, posted on Farrell's site); worth reading as the compact statement of the view that large models are not agents but a new cultural and social technology, of a kind with writing, print, markets, bureaucracies and elections: lossy summaries of what other humans have produced that let people reorganize it at scale. It is a four-page Policy Forum argued by analogy, with no data. Its one mechanism with consequences is that models fit their training distribution on average, so are least accurate where the data are rare, which may homogenize culture; it sets this against the possibility of "society-like" ecologies of models that keep diversity. |
| [LIT-896](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-896.md) v2 | AI as Agency Without Intelligence: on ChatGPT, Large Language Models, and Other Generative Models | Floridi (2023), DOI-10.1007/s13347-023-00621-y. A seven-page editorial. LLMs "do not think, reason or understand" and work statistically on the form of texts, not their meaning, yet they act successfully and, through reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, "learn" to improve. So they are "a new form of agency", one that has been "liberated … from intelligence": Agere sine Intelligere. The thesis is asserted, not argued. No criteria for agency are stated, the only mark that separates it from a sea wave's difference-making is the capacity to learn to make a different or better difference, and the support for "no understanding" is a handful of anecdotal failures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-697](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-697.md)); worth reading as the short first statement of Floridi's slogan that LLMs are "agency without intelligence" (Agere sine Intelligere), which his 2025 paper (LIT-897) develops. Read the last two pages for the thesis. It is an editorial, not an argument. The thesis is asserted in three paragraphs, no criteria for agency are given, and the one citation for the agency notion is Floridi & Sanders 2004 (LIT-898), whose apparatus it does not use. |
| [LIT-897](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-897.md) v2 | AI as Agency without Intelligence: On Artificial Intelligence as a New Form of Artificial Agency and the Multiple Realisability of Agency Thesis | Floridi (2025), DOI-10.1007/s13347-025-00858-9. An Editor Letter that "grew so long". AI is better understood by widening agency to forms without cognition, intelligence or mental states than by widening intelligence to machines. Agency comes in kinds (natural, biological, animal social, artefactual, human individual and social, artificial, social artificial). All of them share interactivity, and the richer ones add graded autonomy and adaptability. AI is computational, data-adaptive agency serving goals set by humans, with no intelligence. The thesis is assumed, and the paper characterises the kind rather than arguing for it. The criteria do not separate AI from other artefacts, and no level of abstraction is stated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-702.md)); worth reading for the fullest statement of Floridi's position that AI is "agency without intelligence": the Multiple Realisability of Agency thesis set against the Artificial Realisability of Intelligence, Floridi & Sanders' three criteria restated as graded, and a taxonomy that places AI as "a computational, goal-driven form of agency defined by human purposes" with Agentic AI as its collective form. Read it as a taxonomy, not an argument. The case for MRA over ARI is announced and not made, since the paper assumes AI is an agent and asks what kind. AI's lack of intelligence is asserted. No level of abstraction is ever specified. Interactivity alone makes a river a natural agent, so the permissiveness objection is accepted rather than answered. |
| [LIT-899](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-899.md) v2 | Faultless responsibility: on the nature and allocation of moral responsibility for distributed moral actions | Floridi (2016), DOI-10.1098/rsta.2016.0112. When a network of human, artificial and hybrid agents brings about a morally loaded outcome through interactions that are each morally neutral, nobody intends the outcome, so an ethics that requires intention holds nobody responsible. Floridi proposes holding every causally accountable node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible" (p. 7), by default and overridably, with the rule made common knowledge so that agents restrain one another. The mechanism is adapted from back propagation, strict liability and common knowledge, and illustrated by two Dutch Supreme Court rulings. It is argued by design and analogy. Its responsibility is causal accountability used as a corrective, not blame, and the paper does not reconcile this with Floridi & Sanders 2004's distinction between accountability and responsibility. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-699.md)); worth reading for the line's one worked rule for who answers for an outcome nobody intended: identify the distributed moral action and the network causally accountable for it, then hold every node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible" (p. 7), overridably, with the rule made common knowledge so agents restrain one another. Read §4 and the two Dutch cases (p. 9). It is a design argued by analogy, not a derivation. Its "responsibility" is Floridi & Sanders 2004's accountability under another name, used as a corrective signal, and the paper never addresses that distinction. In its own boats case the default gives way to ease of rectification, which is a control criterion. |
| [LIT-901](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-901.md) v2 | Distributed Morality in an Information Society | Floridi (2013), DOI-10.1007/s11948-012-9413-4. Distributed morality is the case where morally loaded actions of a human, artificial or hybrid multiagent system result from interactions among its members that are each morally neutral or negligible, modelled on distributed knowledge (A knows P∨Q, B knows ¬P, only the "supra-agent" AB knows Q). Two moral thresholds make environments fault-tolerant to small evils and inert to small goods, so managing distributed morality means aggregating possible goods and fragmenting possible evils. ICTs make it common. "Infraethics" is the first-order framework of moral enablers (trust, privacy, transparency …) that is not good in itself. The analogy is looser than it looks: every example sums like contributions past a threshold whose value is left open. Responsibility for distributed morality is not addressed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-698.md)); worth reading as the line's only worked statement of distributed morality (morally loaded actions of a multiagent system arising from interactions each below a moral threshold) and as the source of "infraethics", the first-order framework of moral enablers that is not morally good in itself. A report in the OECD Public Governance Reviews defining policy capture as the process of consistently or repeatedly directing public decisions away from the public interest toward a specific interest group or person, by legal or illegal means and by that group's intent and action; adopting three criteria (an explicit policy goal, a captor's intent to extract rents, a shift from the goal); and setting out four strategies for preventing it (stakeholder engagement, transparency, independent oversight bodies, organisational integrity). | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1043](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1043.md)), chapters 1 and 2 in full and chapter 3 in part, from the OECD's own PDF; worth reading for its definition of policy capture as consistent or repeated diversion of public decisions from the public interest toward a specific interest, by legal or illegal means, for its three criteria (an explicitly defined policy goal, a captor's intent to extract rents, a shift of the process from the goal), and for its catalogue of vehicles, which includes supplying research and manipulated information, so that capture can proceed without the decision maker's knowledge. | [LIT-1340](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1340.md) v2 | Regulatory independence may limit electoral holdup but entrench capture | Schram & Ule (2024). Where elected policymakers set infrastructure prices, investors fearing electoral pressure delay investment (holdup); regulatory independence, modelled as a price fixed by the first policymaker for all periods, can relieve that, but if policymakers' interests are aligned with the infrastructure owner's ("regulatory capture", assigned as a treatment), independence entrenches the capture. | [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |
